155. **The Diagnostics module takes the console, the overlay's model, the keys and the settings.**
    Both engines carry nearly the same command registry, console host and overlay model, with keys
    that drifted apart, and neither has a registry of settings. The module `3DEngine.Diagnostics`
    holds them once. In steps, each its own commit on main with the suite whole. Step 1, the
    registry. The module comes as a submodule at `modules/Diagnostics`, embedded as the other
    modules are and never a package. The `[Command]` attribute is the module's, the generator stays
    here and emits `Registry.Process.Add` as the module's README says a generator emits, and the
    engine's own command registry, its command and parameter types go; the console host runs a line
    through the module's registry, a late answer written to the console by the host; the Modeling
    module's commands are hosted through its list of commands in place of the engine's own `model.*`
    ones. Step 2, the console, the overlay and the keys. The console's model and its ImGui drawing
    are the module's, the overlay's lines come as sections the engine fills, and the keys are the
    module's actions, F1 hide the interface, F2 screenshot, F3 overlay, F4 settings panel, F5
    console, each a setting a player rebinds, no chord of F3 with F4. Step 3, the settings. Every
    engine value a console command or an environment variable sets today is registered as a setting
    with its range, its default, whether it takes effect at the next start and the variable that
    overrides it, the panel draws them by page, and a game's settings are saved to one file in the
    player's folder through the module's file. A picture of the console and of the panel in a
    running example with each of steps 2 and 3. What the module lacks for a step goes to its session
    in five lines and is mended there, never worked round here. The lighting branch goes on beside
    this.

156. **The Sky module is named Atmosphere, and the marker of Bevy's own atmosphere takes another
     name.** The module's repository becomes 3DEngine.Atmosphere, its assembly and namespace
     Atmosphere and its class Atmosphere becomes Air, by the module's own item. A namespace
     Atmosphere at the root hides a type of that name from a game's plain use, so the marker
     `Bevy.Atmosphere` in Core/Ecs is renamed `Bevy.PlanetAtmosphere`, its native name "Atmosphere"
     unchanged, in the examples, the tests and the feature test with it. That part does not wait and
     goes with the next commit. Once the module's commit is on GitHub the bridge follows in one
     commit. The submodule moves from modules/Sky to modules/Atmosphere with the new address, the
     project references and the package's embedded assembly take the name, each `using Sky;` becomes
     `using Atmosphere;`, and the module's type Atmosphere becomes Air where the bridge names it.
     The guides, the cheatsheet and the README's module table take the name. The pin moves 69
     commits with the rename, so the bridge's sky light changes with it. The tests' figures move to
     the module's, each named in the Reply with its old and new figure, no bound widened, and a
     sheet shows the feature test's day, sunset and night at the old pin and the new with a
     difference panel.

157. **Both merges of the module measured in the target scene.** The module gains a second merge, by
    line of sight and agreement, beside the one the bridge runs. Once its commit is on GitHub the
    bridge takes the pin, keeps its merge as the default, and reads its target scene under each
    merge against its traced reference, the same parts and views as its last table, with the whole
    GI's time under each. No change of the default goes with it. The two tables go in the Reply and
    a sheet shows the scene under each merge with the reference and difference panels. The merge
    nearer the reference at a like cost in both engines stays as the module's only one.

158. **Escape goes to what is open first.** Where an example, a template or the feature test ends
    the program on Escape, an open console, settings panel, overlay page or text field takes the key
    first and the program does not see it. With nothing open an example may still end on Escape, and
    a game or a template ends on no key unless it sets one. A test holds for the feature test that
    Escape with the panel open goes back a page and the window stays, the guides and the cheatsheet
    say it, and it goes with the held commit's follow-up or as a small commit of its own.

159. **An open console or settings panel holds all input from the program.** With the settings panel
    open, the pad and the keys that change a row also drive the scene behind it. The Diagnostics
    module answers whether a panel that takes input is open, and while it does the bridge's input,
    keyboard, pointer, wheel and pad, reads to a program as though nothing were pressed or moved.
    The overlay holds nothing, the diagnostics' own keys still act, and a held key or stick at the
    moment a panel closes does not fire as a fresh press. A test holds it for the feature test with
    a pad's stick and a key, the guides say it, and it comes with the module's pin as a small commit
    of its own after step 3.

160. **The window's settings in the panel.** The settings panel holds nothing of the window itself.
    A page `window` gains `window.mode` with the choices windowed, borderless and fullscreen,
    `window.resizable`, `window.width` and `window.height` for the windowed mode as two settings,
    `window.monitor` naming the screen where more than one is there, and `window.vsync` where it is
    not listed already. A command of a setting's name gives the name to the setting. Each acts at
    once where the system allows it and says "at the next start" on its row where it does not, they
    are saved with the other settings and applied at the next start before the first frame is shown,
    and a mode the system refuses answers in the console and keeps the one before. Borderless covers
    the screen the window is on with no change of the screen's own mode, fullscreen takes the
    screen's mode. A window not shown has the page read-only. The names and choices are the same in
    both engines. Tests hold each setting's round through the file and the refusal, a sheet shows
    the page and the three modes, and the guides say it. It comes after item 159.

161. **A borderless window takes the size set, in the screen's middle.** Borderless today covers the
whole screen whatever `window.width` and `window.height` say. A player on a large screen sets a
smaller resolution and expects a window without a frame at exactly that size, sharp and one pixel to
one pixel, standing in the middle of the screen with the desktop round it, and not a stretched
picture. So `window.mode` borderless makes a frameless window of `window.width` by `window.height`
in the middle of the screen `window.monitor` names. A size as large as the screen or larger covers
the screen as borderless does today, and that is how a player gets the covering kind. Setting the
width or the height while borderless resizes the frameless window at once and keeps it in the
middle. Windowed keeps its frame and its place, fullscreen takes the screen's mode as before. The
picture is drawn at the window's own size and never scaled to the screen. A test holds the size, the
place and the missing frame at a size under the screen's and the cover at the screen's size, and the
sheet shows a borderless window at a smaller size on a larger screen beside the covering one. The
guides and the cheatsheet say it. The mode has four choices, windowed, borderless, borderless
fullscreen and fullscreen. Borderless is the frameless window at the size set, as above, and a size
as large as the screen is the only way it covers. Borderless fullscreen is a frameless window that
always covers the screen, and it draws the picture at `window.width` by `window.height` and scales
it to the screen, so a smaller size set gives a softer picture at less cost, which some players
choose. The scaling is one filtered copy at the frame's end, with the interface drawn after it at
the screen's size where the engine has that split and with it otherwise, the Reply saying which.
This part replaces the sentence above that lets the size decide the cover between two kinds, and the
sheet shows all four. A setting `window.scaling` chooses how borderless fullscreen brings the
picture to the screen, with three choices. Linear is the filtered copy, soft. Nearest takes each
screen pixel from the one picture pixel under it, sharp, even at a whole ratio such as 1920 by 1080
on 3840 by 2160 and uneven at any other, which its help line says. Integer scales by the largest
whole number that fits and stands the picture in the screen's middle with black round it, every
picture pixel a square block of screen pixels. The default is Linear. The sheet shows the three on
one crop at a whole ratio and at a ratio of one and a half.

163. **The third scaling fills the screen and holds still.** `window.scaling` Integer draws the
    picture at the largest whole multiple with black round it, so at a ratio of one and a half it
    stands small in the screen's middle. The third choice is to differ from Nearest in one thing
    only, that it holds still at an uneven ratio, and it fills the screen as the other two do. So
    Integer goes and Sharp takes its place. Sharp scales the picture by the largest whole number
    under the ratio with no filtering and brings that to the screen's size with the linear filter,
    done in one pass by moving each sample toward its texel's middle. Every picture pixel is then a
    block of even color with one blended screen pixel at most on an edge, the blocks all of one
    width, and nothing crawls as the picture moves. At a whole ratio Sharp equals Nearest to the
    bit, which a test holds, and a second test holds at one and a half that the picture covers the
    screen and that no screen pixel differs from Nearest's by more than a blend of two neighboring
    picture pixels. The choices are Linear, Nearest and Sharp, Linear the default, and the
    black-bordered whole multiple is not kept as a fourth. The sheet replaces the Integer column
    with Sharp at both ratios, and the guides and the cheatsheet follow.

164. **Display resolution, render resolution, aspect and fit, each with a native choice.** The
picture and the display get their own sizes, so a player sets what the display shows and what the
scene is drawn at apart, and every setting defaults to native so that a player who touches none sees
the display's own size throughout. The settings are these. `window.mode` keeps its four choices, and
borderless fullscreen always covers the screen. `window.resolution` is Native or one of the sizes
the screen lists, and any width by height from the console. It is the window's size in windowed and
borderless, the screen's mode in fullscreen, and unused in borderless fullscreen, and it takes the
place of `window.width` and `window.height`. `render.resolution` is Native, which is the window's
size, or a size of its own, and the scene is drawn at it. `render.scale` is a helper and holds no
state of its own. Setting it writes `render.resolution` as that share of the window's size, and
reading it gives the share the two stand in. `render.aspect` is Native or one of 16 to 9, 16 to 10,
21 to 9, 32 to 9, 4 to 3, 1 to 1, 9 to 16 and 10 to 16, and where set the scene is drawn at the
largest size of that shape inside `render.resolution`. `render.fit` says how the picture sits in the
window where the shapes differ. Fit keeps the shape with black bars, Fill keeps the shape and covers
the window with the overhang cut, Stretch covers the window and gives up the shape. `render.filter`
is Linear, Nearest or Sharp and takes the place of `window.scaling`. The interface, the panels and
the overlay are drawn after the picture is brought to the window, at the window's own size, so they
stay sharp at any render size, and the pointer and touch reach the scene through the same placement.
Cameras take the picture's shape and not the window's. Tests hold each setting's native choice, the
helper's write and read, each fit at a shape unlike the window's, and the interface's size under a
small render size. The sheet shows a 4 to 3 picture on a 16 to 9 screen in the three fits, a render
scale of 67% in the three filters with a panel sharp over it, and the page of settings. The guides
and the cheatsheet follow. Where the settings module lacks a kind of setting this needs, the ask
comes to the review and the module's session writes it. Four rules complete it. What was set last
holds when the window's size changes, so after `render.scale` the share holds and the render size
follows the window, and after `render.resolution` that size holds whatever the window does. The
debug panels, the console and the overlay take the whole window always, and a game's own interface
takes the whole window unless the game asks for the picture's area, which one call gives. The aspect
belongs to the picture alone, so in windowed and borderless the window keeps its size and the bars
stand inside it. The render size may stand above the window's, to twice it, the panel offering 50,
67, 75, 100, 150 and 200%, and a picture brought down to the window is filtered smoothly whatever
`render.filter` says, since Nearest and Sharp only bring a picture up. In 3DEngine the scene and the
interface leave their shared pass for this, which is wanted for its own sake. The review's later
choices change three things in the above and stand over it. First, who sets what. The panel's page
shows the mode, the window's size, the render scale and the filter, with the aspect and the fit
under them, and `render.resolution` is a console setting and a call a game makes and has no row.
Second, `render.fit` has two choices, Fit and Stretch, and no Fill, and `render.aspect` lists
Native, 16 to 9, 16 to 10, 21 to 9 and 4 to 3 and takes any ratio from the console. Third, two
settings join. `interface.scale` sizes the panels, the console and the overlay's text by one number
and defaults to the display's own scale factor. `render.fps_limit` caps the frames a second beside
the vertical sync and has an Off choice. The render scale is never changed by the engine itself, and
no dynamic scale is built. One more cut stands over all of the above. There is no
`render.resolution` setting, in the panel, the console or the settings file, and no rule of what was
set last. A game's code keeps it. The picture's typed value carries an optional exact render size
beside the scale, a game sets it with the same one call, and code reads the render size in use at
any time. While a game holds an exact size, `render.scale` is kept but not applied, its panel row
says the game fixes the size, and clearing the exact size brings the scale back. The render size is
always the window's size times `render.scale`, shaped by the aspect, and the scale is a stored
setting of its own and no helper.

## Decisions

Decisions 1 Commits stay local; 2 AGENTS.md's bullet on SHARED.md changes by the project's direction
alone; 3 A picture opens the example's own source, and not Bevy's live demo of it; 4 AGENTS.md's
bullet on NORM.md changes by the project's direction alone, with the exception N 7.4 makes; 5 The
examples written are brought to B 4 a group at a time; 6 A run that fails says what failed in a
page, and the reviewing session is given no log; 7 The page's repeated lines are warnings and
errors; 8 The next package is 0.4; 9 A document a game's author reads names no one who decided; 10
The tests run on macOS as well; 11 Feathers' crate may be enabled, after the other gaps; 12 The free
and pan camera controllers may be enabled, after the other gaps; 13 System font discovery stays off;
14 The sample becomes a feature test; 15 Graphics test scenes come as packs fetched on demand, never
checked in; 16 Every tonemapper here comes to 3DEngine; 17 The embedding is the bridge's own; 18 The
weather is vendored and ported; 19 Bevy 0.20 comes after the deferred batch in flight and before the
other gaps; 20 The crates' word for the upgrade; 21 No document or comment a reader sees names a
person or a session; 22 Content streamed on the go stays in the ledger, and the browser stays out;
23 A run that shows no window makes no sound; 24 A game's session writes what the engine lacks in
`.github/ASKS.md`, here as in 3DEngine; 25 A feature of a crate already in the tree that pulls no
crate in is the working session's to turn on; a feature that pulls a crate in waits on the owner's
word as Decision 11 has it; 26 An insert from nothing over a resource a plugin made, of a type that
reflects no default, is refused and names `Resource<T>`; 27 The README's gallery is one scrolling
row of pictures a group, in Bevy's order of its groups; 28 The bcs skill leaves `.claude` for
`.github/BCS.md`, and the gallery's pictures are one size; 29 The development machine's GPU is named
nowhere a user reads; 30 The examples' counts stand under the Examples heading and on each group's
heading; 31 A vertex stream of the game's own, in both engines; 32 A position is every mesh's, and
the packed data a stream beside it; 33 No development on either engine until every job is green on
every push and pack; 34 Two workflows an engine, build and pack, the same shape in both; the tester
zips and the scene packs are runs on the development machine; 35 Decision 33's gate is the new
workflows; 36 The docs job goes; the repository's links are the suite's to check; 37 Prose is
technical and generic; 38 Development resumes, the bridge completed first and the mends of the
moment made lasting after; 39 The direction of 2026-10-19 on the crates, the order and the mends of
the moment; 40 The README's centered parts are markdown inside a centering block, since nuget.org
draws a README without its HTML; 41 A package's release notes are the commits since the package last
published on nuget.org; 42 The pack workflow publishes through nuget.org's trusted publishing; 43
The reviewer starts the pack runs when a package is due; 44 The review's files are committed by the
batch that comes next, and by the reviewer at most once a day; 45 The feature test lives in the
games folder, as 3DEngine's does; 46 Modeling in both engines, from the kernel to the modifiers,
grid prototyping first; 47 The Actions bill is not weighed; 48 Animated captures as tooling for
documentation and devlogs; 49 A screenshot on F2 in every program; 50 F1 hides the interface and F3
shows the debug overlay, in both engines; 51 3DEngine's radiance cascades come to this engine; 52 A
denoiser for the ray-traced tier of global illumination, beside the cascades, in both engines; 53
The cloud sessions take GPU-free items on branches of their own; 54 Branches are named for their
work, never claude/ or a random string, and work stays on main where one session writes; 55 Every
commit carries the repository's author identity, and the cloud session's branch was deleted for not
carrying it; 56 Slang reads the same in both engines, plain names and no module prefix; 57 Until a
full release, both engines are used by nobody; 58 The two cheatsheets have one form; 59 A devlog
under `.github/devlog`, with AGENTS.md's row for it; 60 A session saves the pictures of its work in
the repository, N 4.8; 61 The feature test's level is redone, the look, the sky, the file, the
entities' connections and an editor; 62 The fog, the clouds and the rest of the weather are written
in the engine, and the weather crate goes; 63 Trees and foliage are grown, not loaded; 64 The devlog
written as the work goes; 65 The devlog carries notes beside the pictures; 66 Free textures ship as
a bounded collection, the models stay reference; 67 The level file is Valve 220 map text; 68 The
feature test's open map is legacy and its features move into one generated level; 69 A reading's
picture explains itself, and a plain capture or pair stays where it shows the thing; 70 Every

and not scheduled; 72 The version's major and minor move by the reviewer's judgment; 73 What a

everywhere; 78 Crowns read thick and filled; 79 Each README cross-references the other engine, each
in full under Decisions in REVIEW-ARCHIVE.md.

80. **No millisecond budget.** Decided on 2026-11-08 at 08:50. There is no millisecond budget. A
   feature is first made to work and to perform well, and its numbers are worked on after or along
   the way as much as possible. So a mend that brings a view to its reference lands by its figures,
   its cost measured and recorded beside them and cut after or along the way where a cut holds the
   readings; item 114 and the rest land or stay by their figures, the cost a figure and not a gate,
   and the forest's and the meadow's milliseconds stay in each record.

81. **A stop rule and one target.** On 2026-11-08 at 08:5x, on the question why the light leaking
   had moved little in days, the direction was that the review does what it thinks right and reports
   it for approval. Approved at 08:49 on 2026-11-08, so a view inside its band lands and a figure
   that remains is recorded and not chased unless it lies in a scene that is looked at, the meadow
   here and Sponza's named views in the engine; one bounded read places a cause and a second is the
   last before a mend is tried or the figure recorded. The meadow at eight in the morning is the
   bridge's one target scene, its crowns and its grass against the one reference, the rooms the
   guard.

    2026-11-08, on item 116's meadow pair, no changes were visible in the comparison, the crossing
    among them, as in the times before, and the ask was that where there is a difference a third
    image to the right show it. From here a reading's pair carries a third panel, the after's
    luminance less the before's at a gain the caption names, brighter in orange and darker in blue
    on black, in both engines (N 4.9); the earlier readings stand as they are. The change 116 makes
    is small, about one point in the leaves and a little more of the crown's scattered light on the
    wall and the ground behind it, which the panel shows at a gain of 40, and it is reported so.

83. **Version tags.** Decided at about 14:00 on 2026-11-08, after every commit of the Unity
    Essentials repositories was tagged as `v2.0.30` and the like, the three projects take tags too,
    with the review's questions answered at 14:1x. The form is `v6.0.91`, the letter v before
    `build/version.sh`'s number. Tags go on each major or minor change and on the commits packages
    were built from, since a tag on every commit clutters the list and is unnecessary, the tags
    marking releases some time apart with meaningful changes and not commits apart. The major and
    the minor are the sessions' to raise, each session working on the project deciding when the time
    is right to raise the minor or the major, every commit counting as a patch, with full liberty
    once a step is done and meaningful changes were made. N 6.3 holds the rule and the reviewer sets
    the tags as it pushes. `v0.6.0` marks the commit that set 0.6 and `v0.6.18` the commit
    `b8cc8316` the package of 0.6.18 was published from on 2026-11-02, both set at 14:12.

84. **No middle dot.** Decided at 17:57 and 18:00 on 2026-11-08, the middle dot is not used, the
    README's top links separated by a space alone and the dot nowhere else; the reviewer changed the
    README's first line in the tree on that decision, for the next commit to carry, and every other
    middle dot in the repository is item 118's. The rule goes into STYLE.md's Punctuation as the
    shared text has it everywhere.

85. **One repository, many projects.** The engines' future was thought through with the review at
    about 18:20 on 2026-11-08, after Unity Essentials, where every feature is a repository of its
    own. The points made were that the engines are somewhat cluttered and should be modular,
    extendable, stable and easy to use, that splitting everything into repositories adds clutter and
    makes commits awkward, that the shared modules' repositories are right, that the engine's own
    content could be made modular the same way inside its repository, and that one running process,
    edited and seen as it changes, is worth thinking about; the review's recommendation was approved
    at 18:30. The direction is that each engine stays one repository and becomes one solution of
    many projects, each an area with its own public surface and its own plugin, packed as its own
    package at one version for all, as Bevy's crates are in Bevy's one repository; the dependency
    direction is held by project references and a norm test over them; the flat API stays unchanged
    on top and a game names the packages it needs; the names are dotted .NET names and not com.;
    there is no editor, and the live path is a watcher that recompiles a changed shader, reloads a
    changed asset or scene and recompiles a changed behavior into the running process, the engine's
    own code by restart. It is scheduled after the current items and done as one mechanical batch
    per engine with the public API held identical before and after and the documents' tables
    redrawn. Items 119 and 120, 3DEngine Decision 102.

86. **Comments on the code's own terms.** A comment of scenes_sponza was read at about 19:00 on
    2026-11-08, "The frame graded as that scene's HDRP profile grades it, by the look of its AgX -
    Powerful.exr, a lookup build/unity-lut.py writes from that strip, a gamma of w 0.225, and a
    bloom of intensity 0.25, threshold 0.333 and scatter 0.7, worked out as HDRP works them out",
    and found to read badly, to read as an em dash does, and to lean too far on outside knowledge
    and on the sessions' knowledge of work in progress, in scenes_sponza explicitly and probably
    everywhere else. The rule from it, in STYLE.md's Register and as N 4.11, is that a comment

163. Done. `window.scaling` reads Linear, Nearest and Sharp, Linear by default, and Integer is gone
with no fourth choice kept. Sharp fills the screen at any ratio as the other two do. A window pixel
inside a picture pixel takes it whole, and one across an edge blends the two picture pixels either
side by the share of its width past the edge, so every picture pixel is a block of one width with
one blended window pixel at most on an edge. At a whole ratio no window pixel crosses an edge, and
it equals Nearest.

The blend is worked out from the ratio itself and not from the largest whole number under it. At one
and a half that number is one, so the picture scaled by it is the picture as it stands, and the
linear filter bringing it to the screen blends every window pixel, which is Linear and leaves no
even block where the item asks for blocks with one blended pixel at most. Moving each sample toward
its picture pixel's middle by the ratio gives those blocks, and at a whole ratio the two ways agree.

The shader reads the four picture pixels round a sample with loads and blends them by the shares it
works out, rather than leaving the blend to the linear filter, because the filter's weights are
fixed point and a sample a float's step from a picture pixel's middle can take a part of the next
one and move a color by a level. A share under half of a 256th is taken as none, which absorbs the
float error of the ratio read from the step across a window pixel, so a whole ratio equals Nearest
to the bit. The linear and nearest scalings keep the sampler, and the sharp one has an entry point
for each of the three color spaces a picture is kept in, chosen when the pipeline is specialized,
since the bridge's WGSL has no preprocessor.
